violated_invariant: A pool's base/quote token addresses must be fixed after deployment; init() must not be callable again (and never by an arbitrary caller) once the pool holds funds.
notes: The exploited contract is the DODO DVM pool 0x051ebd..., whose init() had no initialized guard; inside the flashLoan callback the attacker re-ran init() with two fake tokens so the repayment check measured balances of the fake tokens while the real wCRES/USDT left the pool. Its source was not recovered, and the three recovered candidates (wCRES WrappedERC20, a Gnosis Safe proxy used as maintainer, FeeRateModel) are not the defect location, so no Slither finding can explain the exploit; function names in locations are taken from the PoC call and public DODO code, not from recovered source.

violated_invariant: The NFT contract's init() must run exactly once (by the deployer); ownership and mint/burn rights must not be claimable by an arbitrary caller after deployment.
notes: The 88mph NFT contract's init(owner, name, symbol) was never called after deployment (or lacked an effective guard), so anyone could call it and become owner, then burn and re-mint existing token ids. No source was recovered for the victim and no Slither findings exist, so there is nothing to adjudicate; the file:function names are inferred from the PoC interface, not from recovered source.

violated_invariant: A relayed cross-chain message must never be able to target the bridge's own privileged contracts (EthCrossChainData) or invoke arbitrary selectors from the manager's privileged context; the keeper public key set must only change through the intended governance path.
notes: The defect is in EthCrossChainManager (no source recovered): _executeCrossChainTx let a verified message target any contract, including the manager-owned EthCrossChainData, with a selector derived from a user-chosen method string, so a brute-forced 4-byte collision for putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes replaced the keeper set; the attacker then signed fake unlock messages for LockProxy. EthCrossChainData and LockProxy have source but only contain the correctly-gated onlyOwner/onlyManagerContract code, so none of their findings explain the exploit. LockProxy arbitrary-send-eth [0] is by design behind onlyManagerContract, encode-packed-collision [26] is a false positive because every field is length-prefixed by WriteVarBytes, and uninitialized-local [76] is a struct whose fields are all assigned.

violated_invariant: msg.value may be credited at most once per transaction; a payable multicall that delegatecalls into payable commitEth must not let the same ETH be counted for every sub-call and then refunded from the contract's balance.
notes: The DutchAuction inherited a payable batch() that delegatecalls each encoded call, so five commitEth calls in one batch each saw the full msg.value and the overflow refund logic paid the excess out of the auction's own ETH. This is a design/logic flaw in composing a payable multicall with msg.value-dependent functions rather than a missing require, hence business_logic (input_validation would be the alternative). No source or findings were recovered for the auction contract; names are taken from the public MISO code.

violated_invariant: vVISR shares may only be minted in proportion to VISR actually received by the Hypervisor; the contract supplied as `from` must be a genuine Visor vault, not an arbitrary attacker contract whose owner() and delegatedTransferERC20() return whatever the caller wants.
notes: RewardsHypervisor.deposit accepts any `from` address, and when it is a contract it trusts IVisor(from).owner() == msg.sender and calls from.delegatedTransferERC20() with no check that `from` is a registered Visor vault or that any VISR arrived, so a fake vault minted 100M vVISR for free. The raw DHL label says reentrancy, but the PoC and code show no reentrant call; this is unvalidated trust in a caller-supplied contract. Slither's arbitrary-send-erc20 [0] is a real issue (anyone could pull VISR from an approved EOA via the else-branch) and sits in the same function, but it describes the safeTransferFrom branch, which has allowance protection, not the exploited delegatedTransferERC20 branch, so it does not explain the exploit; [16] is a harmless name shadowing.

violated_invariant: A contract that holds users' ERC20 allowances must never execute a caller-chosen call target with caller-chosen calldata; the exchange call must be restricted to a whitelisted 0x exchange and must not be able to invoke transferFrom on behalf of the writer.
notes: ACOWriter.write lets the caller pass exchangeAddress and exchangeData, and _sellACOTokens does _exchange.call(exchangeData) with no restriction, so with a mock ACO token the attacker made ACOWriter call USDC.transferFrom(victim, attacker, amount) using allowances users had granted to ACOWriter. Slither only reports an informational low-level-calls [4] on that exact call; it is a true statement about the dangerous line but the detector does not describe the weakness (user-controlled target and data), so it is valid but does not explain the exploit. The other findings are style, solc-version and constructor zero-checks.

violated_invariant: fnftsCreated (the next FNFT id) must be advanced before any external callback during a mint, so a reentrant depositAdditionalToFNFT cannot obtain the id of the FNFT series currently being minted and attach a deposit amount to it.
notes: FNFTHandler.mint calls ERC1155 _mint (which invokes onERC1155Received on the recipient) before incrementing fnftsCreated; during the callback for the 360000-unit series the attacker called depositAdditionalToFNFT on the earlier FNFT, whose getNextId() still returned the id of the series being minted, so one 1e18 deposit was recorded as the per-unit amount for all 360000 units, which were then withdrawn. Slither reentrancy-benign [46] names exactly that function, that external call and 'fnftsCreated += 1' written after it, which is the exploited weakness despite the 'benign' label, so it explains the exploit. [45] is the same ordering bug in mintBatchRec (real, not the path used), [58] is a genuine tautology, and [47] (reentrancy-eth in doMint via trusted WETH) is noise.

violated_invariant: Voting power used to pass and execute a BIP must not be obtainable within a single transaction; an emergency commit path that executes arbitrary diamondCut/init code needs a timelock or snapshot-based voting so flash-loaned Stalk cannot reach the supermajority.
notes: The attacker proposed a BIP whose init contract transfers the Silo's assets, waited the 24-hour emergencyCommit delay, then flash-loaned ~$1B of stables to mint BEAN3CRV, deposited it for instantly-counted Stalk, and called emergencyCommit, which executed the proposal via the diamond's init delegatecall. The defect is in the GovernanceFacet (vote weight from current deposits, no timelock on the emergency path), which is not among the recovered candidates; the recovered Diamond proxy, LibDiamond and Bean token are only forwarding/affected code, so no finding can explain the exploit. Diamond unused-state [37] is a false positive: AppStorage s is the diamond's shared storage anchor used by the facets.

violated_invariant: A borrower's accountBorrows must be recorded before any value is sent to the borrower; while a borrow is in flight the borrower must not be able to call Comptroller.exitMarket and withdraw the collateral backing that borrow.
notes: borrowFresh sends the borrowed ETH via Fuse's CEther.doTransferOut (to.call.value with unlimited gas) before writing accountBorrows; in the receive() hook the attacker called Comptroller.exitMarket, which read a zero borrow balance and released the fUSDC collateral, which was then redeemed. The CEtherDelegator candidate bundles the logic source, so its findings apply. reentrancy-no-eth [430] flags exactly this function, the accountBorrows writes after an external call and the cross-function reentrancy through borrowBalanceStoredInternal that exitMarket relied on, so it explains the exploit, with the caveat that Slither attributes the external call to the comptroller hooks because doTransferOut is abstract at the CToken level and it never sees the ETH send; confidence is medium for that reason. [397] and [434] are the same ordering issue seen through totalBorrows and the borrowInternal wrapper; [427]/[433] about the nonReentrant helper are noise.

violated_invariant: The proxy's own state (proxyAdmin) must not share storage slot 0 with the implementation's Initializable flags; initialize() on Governance, Staking and DelegateManager must be callable only once and never by an arbitrary caller after deployment.
notes: AudiusAdminUpgradeabilityProxy declares `address private proxyAdmin` as an ordinary state variable (slot 0) while the implementations inherit OpenZeppelin Initializable whose `initialized`/`initializing` booleans also live in slot 0; the second-lowest byte of the admin address made `initializing` read as true, so the initializer modifier always passed and the attacker re-initialized Governance (registry = self, votingPeriod 3, quorum 1%, guardian = self), Staking and DelegateManagerV2, gave himself 1e31 delegated stake and passed a proposal transferring AUDIO out of the governance treasury. The Governance logic candidate 0x1c91af... was deployed at block 15203848, after the fork block 15201793, so it is post-patch and excluded; pre-patch Governance code is present inside the flattened Staking/DelegateManagerV2 bundles. No Slither detector models proxy-vs-implementation layout, so nothing explains the exploit; the ______gap shadowing-state findings are the standard OZ upgradeable gap pattern and are false positives, while the proxy's missing zero-checks are real but minor.
